title: The lens that makes learning click
skeleton:
Picture [topic/concept] as [plain-language analogy].
That perspective can make [desired outcome] easier to reach.
beats: Connect the image to a practical payoff
why: A vivid analogy makes an unfamiliar idea easier to grasp and ties that understanding to a clear benefit.

title: Turn a Sticking Point Into a Starting Point
skeleton:
[Audience] shouldn’t have to [recurring frustration] to reach [desired outcome].

I know because [brief moment you faced the same challenge]. Back then, [specific obstacle] made progress feel [emotion].

Since then, [what has changed]. Now, [audience] can [new opportunity] without [common barrier].

A practical place to begin:
- [First useful action]
- [Second useful action]
- [Third useful action]

The hard part is [honest roadblock]. Even so, [why taking action is worthwhile].

I created [resource or offer] to help you [specific result]. It includes [distinctive value]. To get access, [simple CTA].
beats: Show how the landscape has shifted
Offer a few concrete starting steps
Acknowledge friction and reaffirm the benefit
Present a resource and invite action
why: A personal-to-practical progression builds trust before making the offer feel like a useful next step.

title: Make the lesson useful beyond its usual audience
skeleton:
[Skill or principle] can help far more than [usual audience or situation].

People aiming for [desired outcome] rely on it because it makes [specific benefit] possible.

A simple way to apply it:
[Practical approach 1]
[Practical approach 2]
[Practical approach 3]

The key is [central takeaway]. Put it into practice and you can [concrete result].

Try [small next step]. [Invite readers to share their experience or close with a brief sign-off].
beats: Broaden who the lesson applies to
Connect it to an aspirational outcome
Close with an action or invitation
why: Reframing the audience creates relevance, while practical guidance turns the lesson into something readers can use.

title: A Career’s Worth of Tactics, Sorted
skeleton:
After [time in your field], I’ve learned which approaches don’t hold up.

[An approach that consistently falls short]
[Another approach that misses the mark]
[A third approach that underdelivers]
[A fourth approach to leave behind]

These are the practices I’d stand by:

[A reliable practice]
[Another dependable practice]
[A third practice with lasting value]
[A fourth practice worth repeating]

What’s been true in your experience?
why: The contrast between accumulated experience and two clear lists makes the advice feel grounded and easy to apply.

title: The Attempt That Changed the Pattern
skeleton:
[Drop into a vivid moment from your story when the usual approach failed.] Until then, I had been [old approach], expecting [expected outcome]. Instead, [specific setback].

I decided to try [different approach] because [reason]. The result: [measurable outcome], versus [baseline].

The numbers were useful. The more important discovery was [lesson]. [Explain what caused the difference].

This matters beyond my situation. If you're [reader's related challenge], [show how the lesson applies].

Try [practical first step]. What have you found works when [relevant challenge]?
beats: Contrast the old approach with a new attempt
Apply it to the reader and invite a response
why: A specific setback followed by a measurable shift makes the lesson feel earned and gives readers a clear way to apply it.

title: Make Your Advice Earn Its Authority
skeleton:
A [senior role] dealing with [specific challenge] asked me: “[their question]”

I’ve worked on [relevant area] for [time or context], including [measurable result that shows experience].

My short answer: [recommendation], provided [essential condition].

Before you [take the next step], focus on:
- [specific action]
- [specific action]
- [specific action]

When [essential condition] is missing, [concrete consequence]. That’s why [core lesson].

How do you approach [related challenge]?
beats: Show the cost of ignoring the condition
Close with the principle and invite discussion
why: Pairing grounded expertise with a useful caveat makes the advice feel credible rather than absolute.

title: The Hidden Signal Behind Their Goal
skeleton:
When [audience] says they want to [goal] because [reason one],
[reason two]—or [reason three],
I recognize [underlying challenge].
why: A confident diagnosis turns familiar explanations into a signal of a deeper problem.

title: Make the Milestone Mean Something
skeleton:
I’m [personal detail], and recently I [specific result or milestone].

That moment matters because [purpose behind the work]. I help [audience] move toward [meaningful outcome].

The progress came from [key practice]:
[Concrete action]
[Concrete action]
[Concrete action]

I know the value of that approach firsthand. I used to [earlier situation]; now I [what has changed].

If you’re working toward [related goal], try [small first step]. What’s one move you could make this week?
beats: Open with personal context and a measurable milestone
Connect the achievement to a larger purpose
Show the practical work behind the progress
Contrast an earlier situation with the present
Offer a small next step and invite reflection
why: A personal result earns attention, while the visible work and reflection make the lesson useful to others.

title: Turn a Strong Opinion Into a Useful Playbook
skeleton:
[Common belief] sounds convincing, but [alternative approach] can help you [desired result].
Use these moves to put it into practice:

- [Practical move]
↳ [Specific way to apply it].
- [Practical move]
↳ [Specific way to apply it].
- [Practical move]
↳ [Specific way to apply it].

Keep clear of these traps:
- [Pitfall]
↳ [Why it gets in the way].
- [Pitfall]
↳ [Why it gets in the way].
- [Pitfall]
↳ [Why it gets in the way].

[Takeaway about the bigger value of this approach].
[Question inviting readers to assess their own habits].
“[Relevant quote]” — [Attribution]
beats: Show the upside of another approach
Offer practical steps with brief applications
Name pitfalls and explain their costs
Close with a broader lesson, reader question, and quote
why: Pairing concrete guidance with cautions makes the advice easier to use and harder to misapply.

title: Start With the Part Nobody Measures
skeleton:
[Counterintuitive opinion about a familiar practice].

Most people focus on [visible measure]. I used to, too.

For [time period], I [specific behavior]. Then [moment or result] made me question it.

What matters more is [neglected factor]. Without it, [popular tactic] tends to [failure]. With it, [different outcome].

Now I [changed action]. [Concrete evidence from experience or observation].

Before you [usual next step], try [small corrective move]. What might change if you started with [new priority]?
why: A personal pivot makes the contrarian claim feel earned, while the reframe gives readers a useful next step.

title: The Latest Funeral for [Category]
skeleton:
[New development] is supposed to make [category] obsolete. The most dramatic version of the claim: [doom prediction].

This isn't the first obituary. In [year], [person or source] forecast [earlier collapse]. What followed was [actual outcome].

Look at [historical analogue]. [Evidence or statistic showing what happened]. [Another observation that challenges the forecast].

The mistake is defining [category] as [narrow definition]. A better definition is [broader definition]. When [new development] changes [activity], it can create [new opportunity] rather than erase [category].

So this isn't [doom framing]. It's [more useful reframe]. [Category] is adapting, not disappearing. What are you seeing?
beats: State the current threat in its most dramatic form
Use a past analogue and evidence to challenge the forecast
Redefine the category and explain how the new development can support it
Reframe the threat and invite readers to respond
why: A historical comparison makes a sweeping prediction easier to question, while a sharper definition turns the rebuttal into a more useful reframe.

title: A launch note built around the reader’s gain
skeleton:
[Brief personal opening]: [offer] is ready to use.

For [target audience], it turns [pain point] into [desired result]. Its distinctive approach is [unique value].

Inside, you’ll find:
[Offer detail]
[Offer detail]
[Offer detail]

I made this to [purpose or mission]. It’s a strong fit for [use case or audience].

Take a closer look: [link]. [Direct invitation or next step].

[Suggested image or demo]
beats: Connect it to an audience need
why: Pairing a clear audience benefit with a concrete invitation makes promotion feel useful rather than self-focused.

title: The Benefit Beneath the Benefit
skeleton:
For [target audience], [essential resource] is a must-have.
Its real value goes beyond [obvious payoff].
why: Pairing a clear recommendation with an unstated deeper payoff creates curiosity and makes the advice feel more valuable.

title: Lead With the Outcome
skeleton:
In [timeframe], I [delivered measurable result] for [audience].
The key move was [specific approach].
why: A specific result earns attention, while hinting at its cause gives readers a reason to keep going.

title: The Instant the Outcome Changed
skeleton:
[Serious consequence] became unavoidable
when [trigger event].
beats: Reveal the moment that made it clear
why: Leading with certainty creates tension, while withholding the trigger gives readers a reason to continue.

title: The Turnaround Behind the Outcome
skeleton:
[Person or team] started at [baseline] in [timeframe], aiming for [goal].

Then [specific constraint or setback] threatened the plan. [A detail that makes the stakes tangible].

We chose [approach] because [reason it fit]. The work moved through:
- [Action and purpose]
- [Action and purpose]
- [Action and purpose]

By [elapsed time], [person or team] reached [quantified outcome], moving from [before state] to [after state]. [Additional evidence or milestone].

The useful lesson: [principle others can apply]. If you're working toward [related goal], [invitation or call to action].
beats: Establish the starting point and goal
Share a lesson and invite engagement
why: A clear before-and-after arc makes the method credible while giving readers a principle they can apply.

title: Turn an Industry Saying Into a Practical Lesson
skeleton:
[Familiar saying or joke people repeat in your field]

*[Your candid response to hearing it]*

[Describe a messy moment from your work in 2–3 sentences.]

What did that teach me?

[State one useful action in a single line.]
[Explain briefly how to put it into practice.]
beats: Open with a familiar industry saying
why: A familiar phrase creates recognition, while a specific moment turns the joke into a memorable, practical lesson.

title: Question the Comfortable Assumption
skeleton:
[Number] [familiar beliefs or habits] that deserve a second look:

[Widely accepted example]

[Brief reason to question it]
beats: Introduce a numbered set of ideas to reconsider
Give a concise reason for doubt
why: A familiar example creates recognition, while a brief challenge opens a gap that invites readers to reconsider their assumptions.

title: The Advantage Nobody Sees
skeleton:
The [standout group] don’t get ahead through [obvious strength].
It isn’t their [second strength] or their [perceived edge].
The difference is [unexpected factor].
why: Repeatedly ruling out expected explanations builds curiosity before the final reframe.

title: The Release Gap
skeleton:
[Latest platform/tool/version] compared with [previous platform/tool/version]
(Now featuring [new capability])
beats: Contrast it with the previous release
why: A clear side-by-side contrast makes the change easy to grasp at a glance.

title: A Repeatable Result, Backed by Clients
skeleton:
My go-to 3 [practices] make [desired result] a regular part of my work.

I’ve seen them deliver for [client type], too.
beats: Connect them to a consistent result
why: Pairing a confident personal claim with client validation makes expertise feel credible rather than self-declared.

title: A Faster Route Past the Sticking Point
skeleton:
Want to [reach a specific outcome] without [common obstacle]?
Use these [number] [practical actions] to move forward in [timeframe]—even when [constraint].
beats: Name the desired outcome and obstacle
Offer numbered actions with a timeframe
why: Pairing a clear goal with a realistic path makes the advice feel immediately useful and attainable.

title: The Feeling Behind the Routine
skeleton:
Has [part of your work] started to feel like [frustrating experience]?

Do you find yourself settling for [current reality] when what you want is [better possibility]?

I know that feeling—I’ve been there.
beats: Ask whether a familiar work activity feels frustrating
Contrast the accepted reality with a desired possibility
Build rapport through a brief personal admission
why: A relatable question earns attention, while a small admission makes the reader feel understood.

title: The Move I Regretted
skeleton:
[Time ago], I [made a bold career or life change] so I could [start something new].

I got it wrong.

[Name the concrete reason it failed].
beats: Set a time and personal turning point
why: A sharp reversal creates tension, while a concrete explanation makes the story feel credible.

title: The Questions That Reveal Your Edge
skeleton:
Get [number] questions right, and you may have [valuable outcome] already.

1. [First question]? ([Brief context])
why: A concrete challenge paired with a promised payoff creates curiosity and invites readers to test themselves.

title: The Long-Awaited Reveal
skeleton:
Hello, [community]—I’m excited to introduce [project].
It’s been [time invested] in the making.
why: Pairing a warm announcement with a hint of sustained effort makes the reveal feel personal and earned.

title: Turn a Surprising Experience into a Better Playbook
skeleton:
[A recent experience] made me rethink how people approach [related activity].

Some popular methods can backfire:
1. [Ineffective approach]. [Why it falls short].
2. [Ineffective approach]. [Why it falls short].
3. [Ineffective approach]. [Why it falls short].

A stronger route would be:
1. [Better approach]. [Why it helps].
2. [Better approach]. [Why it helps].
3. [Better approach]. [Why it helps].

The lesson: [Core takeaway about choosing a more effective approach].
beats: Open with a surprising personal experience
Introduce the activity it puts in a new light
Show several ineffective approaches and explain their drawbacks
Pivot to a more constructive method
Offer corresponding better approaches with brief reasoning
why: The contrast turns a personal experience into practical advice by showing what to avoid before offering a clearer alternative.

title: Turn an expert’s work into a practical guide
skeleton:
[Expert] achieved [notable result] in [field]. Their [resource] offers a useful path to [specific skill]:

1. [Actionable insight from the resource]
2. [Actionable insight from the resource]
3. [Actionable insight from the resource]
4. [Actionable insight from the resource]

Explore the complete [resource type]: [link]
beats: Introduce an expert and notable achievement
Name the skill readers can learn
why: Specific takeaways make someone else’s expertise immediately useful, while the source link lets readers explore further.

title: When Yesterday’s Playbook Stops Working
skeleton:
[Legacy approach] was designed around [conditions of the past].

Now, [today’s reality] calls for a different response.

If you want to [specific outcome], move toward [updated approach].

Begin by [concrete action that puts the new approach into practice].

That shift can help you [practical benefit].

What would you change first? [Short line contrasting the old and new ways]
beats: Introduce the legacy approach and its original context
Show why current conditions have changed
Connect the desired outcome to a new approach
Name the benefit of changing course
Invite a response and add a concise contrast line
why: The contrast between an outdated model and present-day needs makes the case for change clear and actionable.

title: A Few Details Beyond the Job Title
skeleton:
My profile covers what I do. It leaves out [number] parts of who I am:

1. [Personal detail]
2. [Personal detail]
3. [Personal detail]
4. [Personal detail]
5. [Personal detail]

Skipping work talk for a moment: what’s one detail about you that rarely comes up?
beats: Contrast professional profile with personal identity
Share a numbered list of lesser-known details
Invite readers to share a personal detail
why: A small personal reveal makes the post feel approachable and gives readers an easy way to join the conversation.

title: The Window Before the Rules Change
skeleton:
[Emerging shift] could create the kind of opening last seen around [earlier turning point]. Right now, just [percentage] of [relevant group] are acting on it.

This is a structural change, not another [category] conversation. [Tool or trend] now lets [audience] [new capability]. When you [specific action], [bold implication].

I expect [vivid future scenario] within [time horizon]. A useful way to read this moment: [guiding principle].

If you’re [audience segment], [specific move].
For [another segment], [specific move].

A practical starting point:
- [First step]
- [Second step]
- [Third step]

[Restate what is at stake and invite the reader to act].
beats: Frame a major opening through current and past shifts
Distinguish the change from ordinary commentary and explain its capability
Paint a specific future and offer a lens for understanding it
Give different audiences a next move
List starter steps and close on the opportunity
why: A vivid forecast feels actionable when it is grounded in a present shift and translated into concrete next steps.

title: A Small System for Getting Past the Usual Roadblock
skeleton:
I [reached a specific outcome] while dealing with [constraint]. The turning point was [brief personal moment].

I turned what worked into [framework name]. It helped me [measurable result].

1. [Stage name]
[Explain the first action and its purpose]. Check: [test for whether it’s working].
2. [Stage name]
[Explain the next action]. Check: [test for whether it’s working].
3. [Stage name]
[Explain the final action]. Check: [test for whether it’s working].

The key wasn’t [common approach]; it was [core principle]. Try [framework name] for [time period] and track [signal of progress].

What would you apply this to? [Invite a response or offer a next step].
beats: Open with a result achieved despite a constraint
Name the method and establish its proof
Explain the framework in ordered stages with checks
Contrast the core principle with the common approach
Suggest a trial and close with an invitation
why: A concrete result earns attention, while a named and testable sequence makes the lesson easy to remember and try.

title: Proof Without the Premium Budget
skeleton:
[Challenge a belief about what success requires]. It’s tempting to blame [missing resource]. But [restate the belief].

Here are a few ways we reached [goal] with less:
Instead of [conventional investment], we [scrappy alternative]. Cost: [amount]. Outcome: [result].

Rather than [another standard option], we [unexpected tactic]. Cost: [amount]. Outcome: [result, with a personal detail].

My rule: [core philosophy]. You can [achieve goal] without [assumed requirement]. Start by [practical action]. Then [next action].

That’s what I enjoy about [field]: whether [scenario A] or [scenario B], we can still [desired outcome]. “ [relevant quote] ” — [attribution]
beats: Name and reject the usual excuse
Show low-cost alternatives with costs and outcomes
State the principle and give practical direction
Close with adaptable confidence and a quote
why: Concrete, low-cost proof makes the contrarian claim credible, while the practical takeaway turns the case study into a reusable lesson.

title: The Permission-to-Act Post
skeleton:
[Audience], here's a perspective worth keeping close:

Many people assume [misconception].
A more useful way to see it: [reframe].

Choosing to [action] doesn't mean [feared interpretation]. Holding back can instead lead to [cost].

This won't fit [exception or context], and that's fair. For everyone else, [reason it matters].

You don't need to feel [doubt] or [shame] to begin. Your ability to [strength] already counts.

What's your experience with [topic]? [Invitation to respond].
beats: Name a common belief and offer a reframe
Defend the action and show the cost of avoiding it
Reassure readers and affirm their capability
why: Pairing a reassuring reframe with a low-pressure invitation makes readers feel both understood and ready to participate.

title: Turn a Visual Pattern Into a Practical Framework
skeleton:
What connects these [count] [visual examples]?

Each expresses [shared principle]. I call this approach [framework name]. Together, they point to [broader meaning]. With [current pressure] reshaping [field], this matters because [reason].

[Example 1]: [short interpretation]
[Example 2]: [short interpretation]
[Example 3]: [short interpretation]

The principle underneath: [key idea]. [Audience] often struggle when they [common mistake].

By applying [framework name], [client or group] achieved [measurable outcome] over [time period].

The takeaway: [lesson]. Put [framework name] to work by [specific action].
beats: State the underlying principle and common mistake
Prove value with a result, then close with a lesson and action
why: Naming the pattern behind familiar examples makes an abstract idea concrete, memorable, and actionable.

title: Build Your Cushion Before the Shift
skeleton:
[Recent setback, stated plainly]. [Contrasting development soon afterward].

In [timeframe], [affected group] absorb [specific cost], while [other group] gain [specific upside]. [Blunt principle]. [Brief line that sharpens it].

The [proactive group] aren't [reactive behavior]. They've built [practical advantage], including [first example] and [second example]. They also have [intangible asset]. When [trigger event] arrives, [specific safety net] is already in place.

That's what [underlying principle] changes. The strongest [career/business] move now is [recommendation].

Starting from [baseline]:
1. [Practical step]
[Specific guidance].
2. [Practical step]
[Specific guidance].
3. [Practical step]
[Specific guidance].
[Question or call to action].
beats: Show who loses and who benefits
State and reinforce the core belief
Contrast reactive people with proactive ones
Name the advantage and its safety net
Close with a question or call to action
why: The contrast makes an abstract principle feel urgent, while practical steps turn that urgency into agency.

title: The case for doing less on purpose
skeleton:
A view worth considering: [contrarian stance].

If you’re [behavior being defended], stop treating it as a character flaw.

You aren’t obligated to [social expectation one].
You can set aside [social expectation two].
You may decline to [expected behavior].

Being in [season or phase] doesn’t mean you’re [label used as criticism].
It may mean [more generous interpretation].

[Explain why this behavior makes sense given someone’s priorities or circumstances.]

[State the takeaway that affirms the choice.]
beats: Release the reader from social expectations
Reframe a criticized phase or trait
why: The permission-and-reframe sequence turns a counterintuitive opinion into reassurance the reader can apply to their own choices.

title: Turn a Quote Into a Better Next Move
skeleton:
[Recognized voice] once put it this way: “[Quote].”

Put simply, [plain-language interpretation].

Rather than [unhelpful impulse], try [constructive response].

Instead of [unhelpful impulse], choose [constructive response].

When [another challenge arises], pause to [constructive response].

When I’m [personal difficulty], I [guiding question or useful action].
why: The quote earns attention, while clear translations and actionable alternatives turn an abstract idea into guidance readers can use.

title: A Small Celebration of the Work
skeleton:
The part of [your work] I enjoy most is [specific aspect].

[Add a screenshot of a client's appreciative feedback.]
beats: Share what you enjoy about your work
why: Pairing genuine enthusiasm with customer praise makes a simple promotional message feel credible.

title: The Three-Part System Behind Consistent Results
skeleton:
After [experience metric], I’ve noticed that [audience] tend to get [poor result] or [strong result] based on [X] core elements.

A [type of entity] relies on:
- [Lever 1] ([category])
- [Lever 2] ([category])
- [Lever 3] ([category])
Leave one out, and [specific downside].

First: [LEVER 1 NAME].
Many [audience] [common mistake]. That can cost [quantified consequence]. Replace it with [better approach], and [positive outcome] becomes more likely.

Then: [LEVER 2 NAME].
Rather than [common mistake], try [approach or sub-framework]. [Brief explanation]. This makes it easier to [benefit].

Last: [LEVER 3 NAME].
A common temptation is to [overreach]. Strong [audience] instead [contrarian action], especially when [qualifying detail].

Which lever would make the biggest difference for you? [Call to action]
beats: Name the three levers and the cost of omission
Explain the first lever through a mistake, measurable cost, and better path
Introduce the second lever, its approach, and its payoff
Challenge a common excess with the third lever
Close by inviting a response or action
why: A clear sequence turns a broad framework into practical advice by pairing each lever with a recognizable mistake and consequence.

title: When the job title understates the impact
skeleton:
A [role A] may be known for [expected value]. Some also become the [role B] people rely on.

They bring more than the basics:
[Additional value 1]
[Additional value 2]
[Additional value 3]

You can see it in how they:
[Positive action with explanation 1]
[Positive action with explanation 2]
[Positive action with explanation 3]
[Positive action with explanation 4]
[Positive action with explanation 5]
[Sum up the difference they make to you or the business]

Know a [role A] like this? Tag them below.
[Call to action]

[Relatable image caption that captures the idea]
beats: Contrast the job title with a bigger role
Name the extra value they bring
Invite readers to tag someone and respond
why: Specific examples turn praise into credible recognition and make it easy for readers to think of someone to tag.

title: The Assumption Worth Revisiting
skeleton:
Maybe [common practice] deserves a second look.

Changing how I [pursue a goal] made more difference than I expected—and it might help you, too:

[Point out the common mistaken assumption].
beats: Tease a personal change and its potential benefit
why: A personal result lends credibility to a counterintuitive opinion and gives readers a reason to keep reading.

title: A Practical Field Note
skeleton:
A closer look at [platform, tool, or topic].

The useful idea: [core lesson or technique].

[Add a brief explanation, caveat, or improvement suggestion.]

[Visual example showing the technique in action.]
why: A focused lesson paired with a concrete visual makes an idea easier to understand and apply.

title: Turn a useful guide into a lead magnet
skeleton:
A practical guide to [topic] for [target audience].

Inside, you’ll find:
- [Section or framework]
- [Section or framework]
- [Section or framework]
- [Section or framework]
- [Section or framework]
- [Additional section]

[Number] ideas, gathered in one [format]. [Number] [audience members] have already [shared or used] it.

Download your free copy: [link]

Which part would you put to work first? [Optional next step]

[Resource preview image]
beats: Preview its contents as a list
Reinforce its value with reach or usage
why: A concrete preview paired with social proof makes the free resource feel valuable and lowers the friction to claim it.

title: Trade the Assumption for Evidence
skeleton:
A common belief among [audience] is:
“[Plausible-sounding misconception].”

The evidence tells a different story:
- [Quantified finding that challenges the belief]
- [Quantified finding that challenges the belief]
- [Quantified finding that challenges the belief]
- [Quantified finding that challenges the belief]

**[Firm statement of the central lesson].**

[Encouraging next step the reader can take].
beats: Present four evidence points against it
why: A familiar misconception earns attention, while concrete evidence makes the correction credible and the final action useful.

title: Beliefs Outside the Mainstream
skeleton:
[Audience] may disagree with me on this:
[Unpopular conviction]
why: A clear contrast with expected opinion creates curiosity before the reader sees the claim.

title: The Scoreboard Isn’t the Work
skeleton:
I don’t use [default measure] as my definition of success.

[Situation 1]? [Brief response].
[Situation 2]? [Brief response].
[Situation 3]? [More generous response].
[Situation 4]? [Encouraging response].

When I [choose or collaborate with someone], I’m not asking them to [preserve the measure].

I’m asking them to [create the outcome that matters]. When that outcome arrives, [default measure] becomes beside the point.

P.S. That’s [the value or principle behind this view].
beats: Separate the choice from protecting the measure
why: The contrast between a familiar yardstick and a more meaningful result makes the opinion feel clear and memorable.

title: The Costly-Scenario Hook
skeleton:
The most damaging [situation] for [audience]:
[A short list of recurring missteps]
Together, they [reveal the underlying problem].
beats: Name a damaging situation for a specific audience
why: A concrete set of mistakes makes the broader lesson easy to recognize.

title: A Small Build, A Bigger Direction
skeleton:
I used [tool A] and [tool B] to create [specific output]. This isn’t proof that [field or role] has no future.

The tools are getting more capable, though [important limitation]. That shift matters because [why progress compounds].

My current workflow can [useful outcome]. It helps me:
1. [Capability] — [benefit]
2. [Capability] — [benefit]
3. [Capability] — [benefit]

[Time ago], my first version of this workflow only [simple function].

Now I’m working toward [larger problem to solve].

What would you want a system like this to handle?
beats: Show a concrete output and the tools behind it
Acknowledge progress and name a caveat
Contrast with an earlier, simpler version
why: A grounded demo earns attention, while the contrast between an early prototype and a bigger goal turns a tool showcase into a story of progress.

title: A Signal, a Take, and a Next Move
skeleton:
JUST IN: [Recent development] is shifting the conversation around [industry or topic].

I’ve followed this closely through [relevant firsthand experience]. Here’s how I’m reading it.

THE UPDATE: [Explain what changed and the key detail].
MY TAKE: [Share an informed reaction or caveat].
THE STAKES: [Connect the change to a broader trend or challenge].

FOR YOU: [Give readers one practical next step].

[Ask a question that invites discussion]. [Offer a relevant follow-up action].

[Suggest a visual that illustrates the development].
beats: Explain the update and offer a take
Connect it to a broader implication
Give readers a practical next step
Invite discussion and suggest a visual
why: Pairing timely news with a credible interpretation and a useful next step turns an update into guidance readers can act on.

title: What the Early Signals Point Toward
skeleton:
[State a specific forecast about your field]. I’m watching to see whether it comes true.

A few signals are shaping that view:
[Describe an emerging pattern]
[Describe another emerging pattern]
[Add one more observation]

[Name an expert or publication] has also reported:
[Share a supporting fact or finding]
[Add another piece of supporting evidence]
[Include one more relevant detail]

If [desired outcome] is the goal, prepare by:
[Give an actionable recommendation]
[Offer another practical move]
[Suggest one final step]
beats: Translate the forecast into practical advice
why: Grounding a forecast in visible signals and credible evidence makes it feel useful rather than speculative.

title: The assumption that made my world smaller
skeleton:
[Audience]: I once believed [limiting belief].
Living by it cost me [time period or missed opportunity].

I saw the impact when [brief personal moment or consequence].

This year, [encouraging perspective that challenges the belief].

The wider picture: [relevant statistic or supporting fact].
[Explain what this evidence suggests].

[Practical, uplifting takeaway for the audience].
[Optional image idea or visual caption].
beats: Name the audience and limiting belief
Show the personal cost over time
Ground the belief in a personal moment
Close with an encouraging takeaway and visual prompt
why: A personal cost earns attention, while evidence and a forward-looking reframe make the lesson feel both credible and useful.

title: The New Label, Old Playbook Post
skeleton:
[Established idea] keeps returning with a fresh label.

[New label] is now all over [publishing format].
“[Advice example]”
“[Another advice example]”

Try the [reasoning test]: what would [beginner perspective] and [expert perspective] both see?
[Answer: the new label describes the established idea].

Much of the [new-label] guidance reduces to that.
It’s [time span]-old [field] presented as a breakthrough.

My take: [brief opinion].
[Question or invitation for readers].
beats: Introduce a familiar idea under new branding
Show the new label and examples of its advice
Apply a test that compares opposite perspectives
Reveal the underlying idea is unchanged
Point out the advice is repackaged old practice
Share an opinion and invite responses
why: The contrast between fresh terminology and familiar substance makes the reframe easy to recognize and gives the opinion a clear payoff.

title: A Casual Meeting, A Useful Exchange
skeleton:
[Unexpected setting] made a welcome backdrop for a conversation about [shared field].

I recently met [person], a [role], after connecting through [context]. When they came to [place], I brought them to [local venue], known for [distinctive detail].

The setting was relaxed, but our purpose had real weight: we both care about [shared mission]. I was curious to hear how [name] approaches the work.

I asked about [professional challenge]. Their advice: [useful insight].
On [another field-related question], they shared [useful insight].
I also asked what they think about [third relevant topic]. Their answer: [useful insight].
For a lighter finish, I asked [personal question]. [Short, humanising answer].

Thank you for the conversation, [name]. [Warm closing thought], and I hope we can [future connection].
beats: Introduce the guest and how you connected
Share three work-focused Q&As and one personal Q&A
Close with appreciation and a future-facing note
why: A relaxed scene gives the reader an easy entry point before the practical insights deepen the conversation.

title: Learn Without the Fancy Credentials
skeleton:
You don’t need [impressive qualification] to [achieve useful outcome].

These [number] [people/accounts] make it easier to get started:

1. [Name]: [What they share and how it helps].
2. [Name]: [What they share and how it helps].
3. [Name]: [What they share and how it helps].

Know someone who belongs here? Tag them. Who should make the next edition? Tell me in the comments.
beats: Lower the barrier to a desirable skill or outcome
Introduce a curated set of helpful creators
List each creator with a short description
Invite tags and suggestions for the next edition
why: Pairing an encouraging reframe with specific recommendations makes the list feel both welcoming and useful.

title: A Setback, Then a Reset
skeleton:
Lately, [current difficulty] has been harder than I expected.

[Describe what makes it challenging, including your private thoughts about it.]

I think back to [earlier time when this felt easier]. [Share a specific moment that shows how it used to go.]

Then, [what made it manageable]. These days, [what has changed]. I feel [honest emotional response].

My plan from here:
[Practical step one]
[Practical step two]
[Practical step three]
[Practical step four]

What’s helped you handle [specific challenge]? I’d love to hear your approach.
beats: Contrast past conditions with the present and share a feeling
Invite readers to share their advice
why: A candid contrast between past ease and present difficulty builds connection, while a concrete plan gives readers something useful to respond to.

title: Turn an Expert Conversation Into a Must-Listen
skeleton:
“[A memorable line that frames a timely concern in everyday terms].”

I joined [guest] for a conversation on [show or platform]. [Guest’s relevant background or distinctive credentials.]

We explored:
— [topic of interest]
— [topic of interest]
— [topic of interest]
— [topic of interest]
There’s plenty more in the full episode.

If you’re [target audience], [reason to tune in]. [Thank or acknowledge a collaborator]. [Invite readers to listen or respond].
[Relevant image or video]
beats: Open with a relatable line about a timely issue
Introduce the guest and where the conversation aired
Tease additional value and address the target audience
Thank a collaborator and invite engagement alongside relevant media
why: A relatable opening earns attention, while credibility and a clear topic preview give the right audience a reason to tune in.

title: A Shortlist Worth Keeping
skeleton:
A practical [number] picks for making progress on [specific goal]:

1. [Resource name] — [creator or authority]
What makes it useful: [recommendation and a revealing takeaway].
2. [Resource name] — [creator or authority]
What makes it useful: [recommendation and a revealing takeaway].
3. [Resource name] — [creator or authority]
What makes it useful: [recommendation and a revealing takeaway].
4. [Resource name] — [creator or authority]
What makes it useful: [recommendation and a revealing takeaway].
5. [Resource name] — [creator or authority]
What makes it useful: [recommendation and a revealing takeaway].

I’ll share more on [related topic] soon. Which pick would you add?
beats: Name the desired outcome and introduce a curated set
Credit each resource’s creator or authority
Explain each recommendation with a useful takeaway
Close with a teaser and an invitation to respond
why: A tightly scoped, attributed roundup makes discovery easier while a specific takeaway shows readers why each pick deserves their attention.

title: A Timeline That Changes the Picture
skeleton:
At [date], [starting point or event].

By [later date], [what changed].

Then, at [another date], [what happened next].

The pattern points to [main takeaway].

This shift can help you [practical benefit].

What would you add to this timeline?
why: A time-based comparison makes change easy to see before explaining why it matters.

title: The Skill Ladder, Then the Missing Piece
skeleton:
Beginner: “I [core task].”

Intermediate: “I [core task] plus [one supporting task].”

Advanced: “I [core task] plus [a broader set of supporting practices].”

Expert: “I [core task] plus [a complete system of supporting practices].”

The reality: “[desired outcome] takes more than [core task].”
beats: Add one action for the intermediate level
Expand the practice set for the advanced level
Reveal that the goal requires more than the basic action
why: A staged escalation makes the simplistic view feel incomplete before the final line reframes what success actually demands.

title: Look Past the Easy Signal
skeleton:
I've encountered [shortcoming] in a [role] during [setting].

I've also seen [strength] in a [role] under [setting].

A [metaphor] may coast on [visible advantage] to reach [outcome], then mistake the ride for skill.

A [capable descriptor] in that same role can make [constraint] the starting point for [meaningful result].

Don't make [important decision] by [obvious proxy].

Weigh [criterion A].
Weigh [criterion B].
Weigh [criterion C].
beats: Contrast shortcomings with strengths observed in context
Show how visible advantage can be mistaken for ability
Counter with someone turning a constraint into results
Reject the obvious proxy for a decision
why: The contrast exposes how easy it is to confuse favorable conditions with genuine capability.

title: The Part That Didn’t Add Up
skeleton:
I found myself in [unexpectedly difficult situation].

It played out through a few patterns:
- [behavior] created [effect]
- [behavior] created [effect]
- [behavior] created [effect]

In [setting], [general challenge] is part of the landscape.

At times, [practical response] is unavoidable.

Still, one piece doesn’t make sense to me:

Why does [specific issue] lead to [larger consequence]?
beats: List its recurring behaviors and effects
Acknowledge the challenge is common in context
Accept a reasonable response may be needed
Ask how the issue produces a larger consequence
why: The contrast between a familiar challenge and its puzzling escalation turns a personal account into a question readers can examine.

title: The Advice That Backfires
skeleton:
Of all the recommendations circulating in [field], this one may do the most damage:
“[Widely repeated advice that leads people astray]”
beats: Frame the field’s advice as questionable
Present it as a direct quote
why: A bold warning paired with a recognizable claim creates tension and invites readers to reconsider familiar wisdom.

title: Let your audience make the first call
skeleton:
We're weighing [important decision], and we'd rather get it right with your help.

[Company] is introducing [first-time initiative] for [intended audience].
[Briefly explain what it is and why it matters.]

A [category] feels incomplete without [audience-desired feature].

Which direction should we take?
[Option A]
[Option B]
[Option C]

Comment with [A, B, or C]. We'll reveal the pick on [date or time] and randomly choose one voter to receive [reward].
beats: Invite help with an important choice
Introduce a first-time initiative and its audience
Name a missing ingredient people care about
Offer options and ask for a vote
Promise a reveal and reward a voter
why: A clear choice makes participation easy, while a promised reveal and reward give people a reason to respond.

title: Milestone Reveal
skeleton:
A major moment: [announcement].

I’ve [personal achievement]—[brief detail that shows its significance].
why: A bold reveal earns attention, while a personal accomplishment makes the news concrete.

title: From First Step to New Reality
skeleton:
[Timeframe] ago, I was [starting point].
After [setback or key decision], I [took a new direction].
Today, I’ve reached [meaningful milestone].
why: A clear before-and-after arc makes the change feel meaningful and invites readers to wonder what caused it.

title: The Choice That Felt Wrong at First
skeleton:
I [made a deliberate choice that reflects a personal value].

Almost immediately, [an event tested that choice]. I had chosen this path because [intended benefit], and [brief context for why the moment mattered].

The experience left me feeling [vulnerable emotion]. My knee-jerk reaction was: “[unfiltered response].”

Then, [short time later], I reconsidered: “[reframing phrase]. This discomfort is part of [reason the choice matters].”

I had hoped for [meaningful outcome]. Getting there also means making room for [uncomfortable feeling].

When [chosen path] never brings up [vulnerable emotion], I may be avoiding the very thing I set out to do. [Takeaway for the reader].
beats: Explain the choice’s purpose and context
Reframe the reaction after a pause
Connect discomfort to the goal and offer a lesson
why: The shift from an honest first reaction to a considered reframe turns vulnerability into a memorable lesson.

title: A Useful Find, Put to Work
skeleton:
[Resource] has earned a place in my [category] toolkit—and it’s [access detail].

Use this [prompt/method] when you want to [desired outcome]:
“[Reusable prompt or method]”

After [time period], I got [specific result].
It also helped me [additional result].

Try it here: [link]

I’m not connected to the people behind it; I’m sharing because [personal reason]. Now I can [next step].

Image note: [what the photo shows].
beats: Recommend an overlooked resource and mention its accessibility
Offer a favorite method for a clear outcome
Show results after a brief interval
Clarify there is no sponsorship and explain the deeper use
why: A concrete demonstration and candid disclosure make a recommendation feel useful rather than promotional.

title: The Win That Exposed a Blind Spot
skeleton:
I [achieved a notable result] in [timeframe].
Then [second proof point that raises the stakes].
I’m [reaction].

What made it more surprising: [context that increased the difficulty]. You’d expect [related business process] to be [reasonable assumption]. Instead, [blunt reversal].

When I examined [area of the business], I found [description of the hidden slowdown]. I was [one cost] while [another consequence].

Here’s what turned up:
- [specific uncomfortable example]
- [specific uncomfortable example]
- [specific uncomfortable example]

The culprit wasn’t [obvious explanation]. It was [underlying cause]. My [audit or reset] isn’t about [surface fix]; it’s about [structural change].

That’s what [Product] is designed to do: [how it works and the outcome it enables]. [link]
beats: Lead with a fast, impressive result
Add a stronger proof point and emotional reaction
Reveal a costly operational flaw with concrete examples
Replace the obvious explanation with the root cause
Position the product as the structural solution and link it
why: The contrast between visible success and a hidden weakness creates surprise, while specific evidence makes the product’s solution feel earned.

title: The operating model behind a measurable AI result
skeleton:
[Business type] now delivers [metric] with AI at its core.

Here are the operating changes behind it:
→ [Workflow]: [how it runs] → [business impact].
→ [Workflow]: [how it runs] → [business impact].
→ [Workflow]: [how it runs] → [business impact].

[Honest assessment of how the approach is working].

Our next focus is [priority]. We’re prioritizing it because [reason].

The takeaway: [lesson].
beats: Lead with the AI-enabled business result
Show three systems and their effects
Name the next priority and why
why: Concrete operating examples make a headline result credible, while the forward-looking priority turns the case study into a useful lesson.

title: The Hidden Cost of the Other Path
skeleton:
[Approach A] and [approach B] may seem like close alternatives. The less obvious cost of choosing [approach B] is [overlooked drawback].

With [approach A], you gain [specific advantage].

If you’re deciding between them, [practical takeaway].
beats: Reveal an overlooked downside of one
why: The contrast makes an invisible trade-off clear and turns it into an actionable choice.

title: The Claim-and-Correction Ledger
skeleton:
What [industry/field] keeps getting wrong:

“[A familiar claim people repeat]”
→ [The less comfortable reality]
“[Another familiar claim]”
→ [The reality behind it]
“[A third familiar claim]”
→ [The blunt correction]
“[A fourth familiar claim]”
→ [What experience actually shows]
“[A fifth familiar claim]”
→ [The sharpest correction]

[End with a pointed question or statement that invites a response].
beats: Set the topic with a judgment
Counter it with a blunt reality
Close with a response-provoking question or statement
why: Pairing a recognizable claim with a sharp correction makes the opinion easy to scan and gives each point a satisfying turn.

title: The workflow shift I wish I’d made sooner
skeleton:
Looking back, I was [using an old approach] to [complete a task].

[Explain how that approach worked and what made it cumbersome].

The result: [specific downside].

Then [time or turning point], I moved to [new approach].
[Describe what changed in the process].

The biggest surprise was [distinctive benefit].

I keep coming back to [tool or resource]. [Tell readers where to find it].
why: A clear before-and-after contrast makes the improvement tangible and gives the recommendation a credible reason to matter.

title: Turn the Detour Into Direction
skeleton:
[Guiding principle]

[Work or life situation] can be demanding, and [kind of obstacle] comes with the terrain. Let [long-term goal] guide your next move.

When [specific setback] happens, [constructive response].
When [another setback] happens, [constructive response].
When [a third setback] happens, [constructive response].

[Relevant quote or piece of wisdom]. Put it into practice by [specific action].

[Short, memorable line for a shareable graphic]
beats: Acknowledge difficulty and orient action toward a goal
Translate the principle into a practical takeaway
End with a memorable graphic line
why: Concrete setback-to-response examples turn an abstract principle into useful guidance readers can apply.

title: The Shorter Route to [Outcome]
skeleton:
I reached [outcome] without relying on [assumed advantage 1].
I reached [outcome] without relying on [assumed advantage 2].
I reached [outcome] without relying on [assumed advantage 3].
I reached [outcome] without relying on [assumed advantage 4].
I reached [outcome] without relying on [assumed advantage 5].

Here’s the simple route to [outcome]:
1. [First useful action].
2. [Second useful action].
3. Keep at it until [desired result].

Most other advice is a detour.

[Visual that reinforces the point]
beats: State the result while naming an assumed advantage you skipped.
Repeat the result-and-barrier contrast several times.
Introduce a simplified route to the result.
Give two practical actions, then emphasize repetition.
why: The contrast challenges assumed requirements, then a compact recipe makes the alternative feel achievable.

title: The Hard Part Still Matters
skeleton:
I don’t always find [difficult action] easy.

Still, it moves me toward [important goal].
why: A candid admission creates connection, while the turn toward a meaningful goal gives the struggle purpose.

title: Birthday Math, Hard-Won Lessons
skeleton:
Today, I’m [target age]—which means I’ve officially outlived my [younger age] expectations.
To mark the occasion, here are [number] lessons I’ve learned about [desired outcome]: …
beats: Reveal age through a playful comparison
Tease numbered lessons tied to a goal
why: A playful personal milestone creates a light hook before promising useful takeaways.

title: A Reading List, Distilled into Practice
skeleton:
After exploring [number]+ books about [topic], I’ve chosen [number] ideas that have genuinely shaped how I approach [area of life or work]:

1. “[Idea or excerpt].”
— [Author], [Book]

2. “[Idea or excerpt].”
— [Author], [Book]

3. “[Idea or excerpt].”
— [Author], [Book]

There are [number] more worth sharing. Want another installment?

Which idea resonates most with you? [Optional call to action]
beats: Preview selected takeaways and their relevance
Present ideas with author and book credits
why: Credible curation delivers useful takeaways quickly, while the promise of more and a closing question encourage engagement.

title: What I value now in [topic]
skeleton:
My perspective on [topic] has changed. Here’s what gets my attention now:

[Old priority] is no longer my measure of success; [new priority] is.
[Old priority] has lost its appeal; [new priority] is what I pursue.
I’ve stopped chasing [old priority] and started investing in [new priority].
[Old priority] used to seem essential; today, [new priority] matters more.
I give less weight to [old priority] and more to [new priority].

What would you add to this shift?
why: Repeated contrasts make the revised viewpoint easy to scan and give the opinion a clear, memorable rhythm.

title: A One-Image Reminder
skeleton:
Keep this [essential idea] in mind:

[Visual that makes its practical impact clear]
why: A direct visual makes an abstract point easier to grasp and recall.

title: A Past Turning Point, Revisited
skeleton:
[A sharp principle drawn from a historic event].

Years after [earlier turning point], [recent development] changed [situation]. Before it, [baseline that shows the contrast]. Yet [key factor behind the shift] helped produce [supporting metric or evidence].

What drove the change?
[Explain the causes with specific people, decisions, or examples]. The outcome: [another statistic or expert assessment].

I see it as [your interpretation or a useful analogy]. Since then, [a consequential follow-up event].

The lasting lesson: [concise takeaway].

[Image concept that reinforces the point]
beats: State a lesson rooted in history
Contrast the past baseline with a recent development
Use a key factor and evidence to show the result
Explain causes and add another proof point
Offer an interpretation and note what followed
Close with a takeaway and image cue
why: Pairing concrete evidence with a historical comparison makes a complex change easier to understand and remember.

title: The Cross-Domain Reality Check
skeleton:
“[Ordinary business expectation voiced as a clueless remark]”

That doesn’t sit right.

You wouldn’t [unfair equivalent] in [a different setting].
beats: Contrast it with unfair treatment elsewhere
why: A familiar comparison makes an accepted business norm look unreasonable.

title: The Long Route to a Breakthrough
skeleton:
When I started [activity], [minimal result] was my only proof of progress.
At [checkpoint], [small win]. Later, [larger win].
By [timeframe], [major result]—and I know I could’ve got there sooner. [number] mistakes I’d avoid now:
beats: Open with a personal pursuit and little progress
Admit the path could have been shorter
why: A compact progress arc earns attention, then turns hindsight into curiosity about practical lessons.

title: Earned Insight, Shared Soon
skeleton:
After [period] of [substantial effort or investment] in [specific activity], I’ve learned what holds up.
Over [short upcoming period], I’ll share [the process or examples] behind it.
beats: Establish sustained commitment to a specific activity
Promise a near-term share of useful practices
why: Demonstrating earned experience before offering practical takeaways makes the promise feel credible.

title: The unexpected edge
skeleton: Top [professionals] gain an edge by embracing [unexpected quality].
beats: Attribute success to an unexpected quality
why: A counterintuitive claim creates friction that invites readers to reconsider what success requires.

title: The Job Title Nobody Puts on a Business Card
skeleton:
A [client] brought me in for [fee] to be their [unexpected role].

They weren’t looking for a [expected professional role].
They weren’t looking for a [second expected professional role].
They wanted a [unexpected role]. (They called it something more respectable, of course.)

Even [high-achieving audience] can [specific struggle]. [Short reason the issue sticks around].

That’s where a [unexpected role] helps: [how this role makes action harder to dodge].

After [first difficult step], [meaningful positive change]. Turns out, [casual takeaway].

Where could you use a [unexpected role] right now? [Invitation to respond or inquire].
beats: Open with a paid, unexpected role
Show that capable people share the problem
Explain how the role prompts action
Reveal the change and invite engagement
why: An unexpected job title creates curiosity, while the concrete struggle and outcome make the offer feel relevant rather than salesy.

title: The Risk List That Turns Into a Lesson
skeleton:
[A costly mistake someone might make]
[A connected risk they may overlook]
[Another consequence that could follow]

The overlooked leverage point is this:
[Unexpected way to reduce or prevent those risks]

Try this first: [specific action the reader can take]
beats: Explain how to reduce the risks
why: Stacking concrete risks creates tension, and a practical reframe turns that tension into useful guidance.

title: After the Applause: A Talk Recap
skeleton:
I’ve just stepped offstage after [talk or event], where I spoke about “[topic or title].”

I joined [event and setting] with [audience context]. I noticed [something memorable about the people or atmosphere].

Ideas I wanted people to leave with:
[Takeaway]
[Takeaway]
[Takeaway]
[Takeaway]

I keep coming back to [specific moment from the experience]. I also made the case that [central idea]. That matters because [what it could change for the audience].

What’s your perspective on [question related to the topic]? [Invitation to respond or take action]

[Photo from the event]
beats: Set the scene and note an observation
State a central idea and explain its significance
Invite the audience into the conversation
why: A personal milestone earns attention, while specific takeaways and a clear invitation turn the recap into a conversation.

title: Readiness Before Resources
skeleton: Until [group] is prepared to [make a specific change], spending more on [familiar solution] is unlikely to help.
beats: Name the group that is not ready
State the change they need to make
Show why added resources won’t solve the problem
why: The formula shifts attention from adding resources to addressing the readiness gap that determines whether they can work.

title: The Milestone After the Long Climb
skeleton:
This is a [defining] day in my [pursuit].
For [duration], I kept [specific effort]. More than once, [challenge] tested my resolve.
Then [sign of progress] came into view. Today, I’ve [milestone].
beats: Name the length of sustained effort
Show a challenge that tested you
why: The formula builds anticipation by stacking sustained effort and difficulty before revealing the payoff.

title: The Goal-Obstacle Paradox
skeleton:
[Goal] can seem out of reach for [group] when [brief difficulty]:

How can you [pursue the goal] with [common obstacle] in the way, when [conflicting condition] is essential?
beats: Name the group and desired outcome
Ask a question that exposes the contradiction
why: A relatable obstacle paired with an opposing requirement creates tension that invites readers to respond.

title: Audience-First Recommendation Hook
skeleton:
For [audience], [resource] is the one I’d point to first.
(If [desired outcome] is your goal, begin here.)
beats: Recommend a standout resource for a specific audience
Invite readers seeking an outcome to explore it
why: A focused recommendation paired with a clear reader benefit makes the opening immediately relevant.

title: The Less Obvious Route to Better Results
skeleton:
To [reach a specific outcome] in [field], try [specific action] before [usual approach].

It may seem counterintuitive—but [brief reason it works].
beats: Recommend an unexpected action over the standard approach
why: A counterintuitive recommendation creates curiosity, while a promised explanation gives readers a reason to keep going.

title: The Lesson Hidden in an Ordinary Moment
skeleton:
[Relatable challenge] taught me more than I expected.
It began when [specific everyday moment].
why: A familiar challenge earns attention, while a concrete moment makes the story feel immediate.

title: Cheap Isn’t the Same as Good
skeleton:
“[Competitor] can deliver [result] [faster/for less]!”

So can [absurd alternative]. That doesn’t make it [quality standard], [name].
beats: Quote a competitor’s speed or price claim
why: An exaggerated comparison punctures the claim and reframes the debate around quality.

title: The Hard Season That Changed My Approach
skeleton:
[Time period] tested me more than I expected.

[How it affected me]. [The specific obstacle I faced].

I responded by [action]. [What happened first].
beats: Show its personal impact and define the challenge
Describe the response and its first result
why: A brief personal arc creates an emotional connection before revealing a concrete response.

title: Borrowed Wisdom, Clear Payoff
skeleton:
My perspective on [topic] shifted most after learning from [person].
[X] lessons from them to help [audience] [desired outcome]:
beats: Credit a person as the strongest source of insight
Preview a numbered set of lessons with a clear audience benefit
why: A specific source of expertise builds credibility, while a focused payoff gives readers a reason to continue.

title: The Habit That Took More Than It Gave
skeleton:
For years, I kept coming back to [relatable habit].
It was taking a toll on [area of life or work]—until [tease of what changed]...
why: A candid confession builds connection, while the cost and withheld turning point create curiosity.

title: Choose a Measure That Fits
skeleton:
[Percentage] of [group] reach [widely admired outcome].

But the popular scorecard is optional. Choose a measure shaped by [personal priority].

Imagine [time horizon] from now: what would make you glad you chose this path?

It might be [expected achievement].

It might be [another personally meaningful outcome].
